title: 30 Things I Hate About Your Game Pitch
location: GDC (likely San Francisco, CA) – venue of the talk
summary: This talk dissects common pitfalls and hard truths about pitching video games, distilling practical guidance into 30 concise observations. The speaker emphasizes pitches should answer two core questions (is the game worth making, and can the team execute it) and warns against overloading a pitch with lore, standard systems, or superficial polish. Key lessons include distinguishing a compelling hook from supporting pillars, clearly describing moment-to-moment gameplay, avoiding heavy backstories and demos that don’t prove the concept, and resisting the temptation to chase the latest tech or a flashy monetization plan. The talk also covers prototyping focus, art direction, dialogue quality, licensing risks, scope realism, and the interpersonal dynamics of working with publishers. The speaker closes with practical tips on preparation, presentation tools, and handling questions, reinforced by examples and counterexamples from industry practice.

title: One-Year Indie Game Launch: Planning, Production, and Self-Publishing (SomaSim's 1849 Case Study)
summary: In this GDC Festival of Gaming presentation, SomaSim cofounder Matthew Vione recounts how his studio planned, produced, marketed, and self-published their first indie simulation game, 1849, within a year (ultimately ~14 months). The talk emphasizes pragmatic project scoping (swag scheduling and the “butchery” cut of features), risk management (sticking to familiar tech), contract and corporate basics, and a multi-faceted self-marketing plan that includes devlogs, social-media outreach, press relations, influencer engagement, and non-game media hooks. The team pursued a cross-platform release (PC and mobile) with careful pricing decisions and localization to boost long-tail sales, while also leveraging early access, DLC, and periodic ads to sustain revenue after launch. The talk culminates with lessons on how to sustain a new studio’s momentum after their first release, and how the second project is structured to avoid over-reliance on the first success.

title: Cursed Problems in Game Design
location: Bay Area, California, USA (Riot Games – Bay Area office)
summary: Alex Jaffe defines curse problems as unsolvable design problems arising when two core player promise conflict, making a perfect solution impossible. He frames curse problems as a clash between an experience (what it feels like to play) and an objective (the game's driving goal), and argues that you must sacrifice part of the fantasy to move forward. The talk provides a practical four-technique framework—Barriers, Gates, Carrots, and S'mores—to manage these curses rather than solve them outright, with applied examples from genres such as free-for-all combat, co-op play, and location-based games. Through a mix of illustrative hypotheticals (e.g., a high-skill, politics-driven fighting game) and real-game cases (No Man's Sky, Diablo III, Smash/PS All-Stars, Journey, The Sims, AlphaBear), the talk guides designers on identifying curse problems early, choosing where to sacrifice, and re-framing games so the core promises remain compelling even as the design shifts.

title: 50 Game Camera Mistakes — camera design deep-dive from GDC Festival of Gaming
summary: This video presents a focused talk on the challenges of designing third-person game cameras, delivered by John Eske (Backend Company) at the GDC Festival of Gaming. Framed around the idea that cameras reveal failures, Eske formalizes a discipline called gamutography and outlines three core camera styles (fixed-angle third-person, dynamic-angle third-person, and first-person). He enumerates and analyzes dozens of failures that can derail camera behavior, illustrates practical remedies (from obstacle-aware whiskers to near clipping safeguards), and emphasizes maintaining player intent and line of sight. Throughout, he uses Journey as a running case study and interleaves cinematic principles (like the 30-degree rule and rule of thirds) with game-specific constraints (seven degrees of freedom; Separation of concerns). The talk also covers player accessibility (simulation sickness, adjustable field of view, screen shake, and input options) and ends with a practical Q&A on tooling and collaboration across disciplines.

title: Animation Bootcamp: Indie Procedural Animation with Minimal Keyframes (GDC 2017)
summary: In this GDC Festival talk, David from Wolfire Games outlines a lean, code-friendly approach to procedural animation for a human-like character in Overgrowth. He starts from a physics-first movement system driven by simple center-of-mass curves and ground-contact rules, then layers detailed animation on top with a small set of keyframes and robust interpolation. The talk covers ground rules that keep movement responsive and predictable, introduces a wheel-like technique to map ground distance to animation, and uses acceleration tilts, pose-driven keyframes, and synchronized blends to blend between walking and running. He demonstrates how to upgrade inter-frame transitions with bicubic interpolation, then introduces a spring-damper system for crouch and landing transitions. The session expands into inverse kinematics (pose matching, multi-joint IK, look targets), secondary physics for subtle bone motion, and even ragdoll concepts and “active ragdoll” ideas inspired by industry work like Euphoria. Throughout, the emphasis is on decoupling animation from core gameplay input, enabling rapid variation with fewer keyframes, and suggesting closer integration of animation with code to offload repetitive work for animators.

title: Fluid and Powerful Animation Within Frame Restrictions — Skullgirls Lead Animator's Techniques
summary: In this talk, Marilla Cartwright, Skullgirls' lead animator, outlines how to achieve fluid, impactful animation within tight frame budgets for a hand-animated 2D fighting game. She emphasizes readability through silhouette, anticipation differences between player and enemy moves, and efficient use of key poses when frame counts are limited. The talk covers practical techniques such as favoring key poses, using follow-through and smears to fill gaps, and employing overshoot and weight-breaking to amplify impact. Cartwright also details Skullgirls' production pipeline—from quick roughs to playable builds to cleanup—and argues that gameplay constraints should drive animation decisions, not hamper creativity. She closes with performance considerations, cautions against over-animation, and recommends reference resources like Zvifus and Fighters Generation to study frame-by-frame animation in fighting games.

title: DOOM: Behind the Music — Change the process to change the outcome
summary: DOOM: Behind the Music is a GDC talk by Doom soundtrack composer Mick Gordon that reveals how the DOOM (2016) score was developed through a radical rethinking of the brief, a culture of collaboration, and hands-on experimentation with synthesis and hardware. The talk traces the path from an initial no-guitars brief through multiple failed approaches, to a process-driven pivot that embraced experimentation, a modular analog pedal pipeline, and even guitar-based textures judiciously integrated via Morph and extended-range guitar. Key themes include fear of rejection as a barrier to change, the value of a failure-friendly team environment (including Weird Wednesday sessions), the use of unusual audio processing (ring-modulated sub-bass, tape echoes, Geiger-counter-like distortion), and the concept of a soundtrack staged as a standalone, tour-able album with deliberately chosen Doom callbacks. The speaker also discusses how game-structure and sound design can be aligned, and how controversy and subliminal ideas were navigated in pursuit of a cohesive Doom identity.

title: 8 Bit & '8 Bitish' Graphics—Outside the Box: Palette, Dither, and Color Cycling

title: The Loners of MMOs: Designing for Solo Play Within Massively Multiplayer Worlds

summary: This talk examines why players sometimes choose to play MMOs solo, reframing the loner as a legitimate and potentially heroic archetype within a social, massively multiplayer space. title: Finishing The First Tree: No Time, No Budget, No Problem — a shoestring indie dev case study
summary: David Whaley recounts finishing The First Tree under extreme time and budget constraints while holding a full-time job, a family, and a partner pursuing art. The talk traces the game’s two intertwined stories, its Steam debut in 2017, and a console port that followed. He explains the core tactics that allowed completion and later growth: leveraging publicly licensed assets and affordable music, adopting a visuals-first, asset-modification approach, and maintaining a daily 1% progress mindset. Marketing was built around consistent GIF-based posts across Reddit, Imgur, Tumblr, and Twitter, with a focus on early assets (website, trailer, Steam page) and data-driven trailer creation using engagement signals. title: Ten Principles for Good Level Design — GDC Talk by Dan Taylor (Montreal, Square Enix)
summary: Dan Taylor’s GDC Festival of Gaming talk distills a holistic, interdisciplinary approach to level design into ten guiding principles. Drawing on classic design theory and practical game examples, he argues that good levels should be fun to navigate, tell stories through environment rather than text, guide players with clear but not prescriptive methods, surprise and empower players, offer scalable difficulty, reward modularity and efficient workflows, embrace non-linearity and emergent play, cultivate emotion, and be driven by core mechanics. The talk weaves in memorable case studies (Mirror’s Edge, BioShock, Hitman, Skyrim, Zelda, Dead Space 2, Halo, Dishonored, Deus Ex: Human Revolution) to illustrate how deliberate spatial design, player agency, and mechanical feedback create engaging, replayable experiences.

title: Failing to Fail: The Spiderweb Software Way
summary: Jeff Vogel of Spiderweb Software offers a long-range, no-nonsense retrospective on building a sustainable indie RPG studio across more than two decades. Grounded in a refusal to chase ‘hits,’ he explains a philosophy of lean development, back-catalog leverage, and remastering as a business strategy, paired with careful cash flow and fan-base cultivation. The talk traces early shareware distribution in the 1990s, the challenges of launching Exile and Avernum titles, the shift to independent publishing with in-house payment processing, and the evolution through Geneforge, Avernum remasters, and new IPs. Vogel emphasizes luck, persistence, the value of owning your source, and the necessity of protecting one’s mental bandwidth from critics while remaining likable to fans. Throughout, he balances practical advice (pricing, contracts, accounting, art workflows) with candid humility about the risks and uncertainties of a long career in an industry that Nobody “knows” yet, while underscoring that quality, consistency, and a loyal fan base can sustain a life as a ‘humble toy maker’ in a brutally competitive market.

title: GDC 2015: Guilty Gear XRD’s NPR Cel-Shaded 3D Art Pipeline
location: GDC stage (Game Developers Conference) – San Francisco, CA, USA
summary: In this GDC talk, Arc System Works technical artist Junior Motomura explains Guilty Gear XRD’s transition from traditional 2D sprites to a cel-shaded 3D look that preserves the series’ anime feel. The talk details the NPR pipeline: tool choices (Unreal Engine 3, Autodesk Softimage), real-time shader previews, and a shader-driven approach that uses vertex colors, thresholds, and reimagined normals to achieve a convincing 2D appearance. Motomura covers outlines and inner-line techniques, two-color texture shading, per-character lighting with no global scene lighting, and a frame-by-frame, limited-animation workflow (roughly 500 bones per character) to retain the iconic 2D appearance in a 3D medium. He frames the ‘X Factor’ as the artist’s intention guiding every step, from modeling to animation, and closes with Q&A on production scale, UV layouts, and future NPR exploration.
